options: A PreToolUse hook that denies the matching call and says why.
A PostToolUse hook that converts results to one unit before the agent sees them.
A PreToolUse hook that rewrites the tool's input into the required form.
A CLAUDE.md rule that explains the convention and the reason for it.

members.stem: A developer-productivity agent built on the Agent SDK must never run git push --force against protected branches. What's the right mechanism?
why: An action that must never happen is blocked before it runs, with a reason the agent can act on.
Right when results arrive in mixed formats. Here the danger is an action, not a result.
Right when a call needs a missing field added. Silently rewriting a force push changes what the developer asked for.
Right for a convention where an occasional miss is cheap. A force push to a protected branch isn't.

members.stem: Three MCP servers report file sizes as raw bytes, “4.2 MB” strings and kibibytes. The agent's cleanup recommendations are often off by orders of magnitude. What's the right mechanism?
why: Right when an action must be stopped. Nothing here should be blocked.
Normalize results to one unit before the model reasons over them.
Right when the agent's inputs need fixing. The problem here is what comes back.
Right for soft conventions. Unit conversion needs to happen every time.

members.stem: Every commit the CI agent makes must include a Ticket: trailer with the issue ID from the job's context. The agent leaves it out about one time in ten. What's the right mechanism?
why: Right when an action must not happen. Here the commit is fine; its input is missing a field.
Right when results vary in format. The problem here is the outgoing call.
A pre-call hook can add the required trailer to every commit, so it's there every time.
Right when an occasional miss is acceptable. Here every commit needs the trailer.

options: Give the subagent's AgentDefinition only the read-only tools it needs.
Pass everything the coordinator already gathered in the delegation prompt.
Have the subagent return its findings in a fixed, structured format.
Write the subagent's prompt as goals and quality criteria, not fixed steps.

members.stem: An “explorer” subagent meant only to map unfamiliar code occasionally edits files while investigating. Where should you fix this?
why: Scope the tools to the role: a subagent can't edit files if it has no editing tools.
Right when a subagent re-fetches what the coordinator has. This one does too much, not too little.
Right when the caller can't parse results. The problem here is unwanted edits.
Right when rigid steps make a subagent inflexible. Prompt wording won't guarantee it never edits.

members.stem: A coordinator delegates “review PR 4812” to a reviewer subagent, passing only the PR number. The reviewer spends most of its budget re-fetching the diff, CI logs and the linked issue, all of which the coordinator already loaded. What fits best?
why: Right when a subagent does things outside its role. This one is just repeating work.
A subagent starts with none of the coordinator's context, so pass what's already been gathered.
Right when results are hard to use. The waste here happens before the review starts.
Right when step-by-step prompts make subagents rigid. The problem here is missing context.

options: Run the same fixed sequence of steps once for each item.
Group the work by root cause first, then handle one group at a time.
Split the input into its parts, process each part separately, then merge.
Let the agent choose each next step from what the previous one found.

members.stem: The agent must generate CRUD boilerplate (model, controller, tests, docs) for 30 similar entities that follow an established pattern. Which decomposition fits?
why: A known, repeated pattern is what a fixed sequence is for: predictable and easy to check.
Right when failures share causes. Nothing has failed here.
Right when one large input hides details. These are 30 small, similar tasks.
Right when the path depends on findings. Here the path is known in advance.

members.stem: A CI agent told to “fix all failing tests” (37 failures across 9 modules) thrashes: a fix in one module breaks tests in another, and runs time out. How should the work be decomposed?
why: Right for repeated, independent tasks. These failures interact.
Fixing by root cause stops one fix from breaking another, and shrinks 37 failures to a few causes.
Right when a long input hides details. Splitting by module keeps the interacting fixes apart.
Right for open-ended investigation. Here, unstructured fixing is what causes the thrashing.

options: A fixed pipeline that runs the same steps in the same order every time.
Separate passes for each document or section, then a step that merges results.
A single agent that decides its next step from each result.
Parallel subagents, one per independent subtask, then a synthesis step.

members.stem: An agent extracts 40 fields from 300-page loan packages that bundle an application, appraisals, tax returns and disclosures. Fields from documents deep in the package are often missed. What decomposition helps most?
why: Right when every case follows identical steps. The problem here is attention over a long input.
Focused passes per document keep attention on each part; the merge step reconciles them.
Right when the path depends on findings. The problem here is coverage of a long input.
Right for independent research subtasks. Fields here are extracted from parts of one package and need reconciling.

members.stem: Every return request follows the same four steps: verify identity, check eligibility, create the RMA, send the shipping label. Which decomposition fits best?
why: When the steps and their order never change, a fixed pipeline is predictable and easy to audit.
Right when a long input hides details. A return request is short.
Right when each step depends on what turns up. Here the steps are always the same.
Right for independent subtasks. These steps depend on each other in order.

options: Return a structured result saying why the call was blocked and what to do first.
Return an explicit pending status that the agent must relay to the customer.
Post a structured handoff: the problem, what was tried and a suggested next step.
Add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to follow the required order.

members.stem: A prerequisite gate blocks update_payment_method until verify_identity succeeds. When it blocks a call, it returns the text “Error.” Logs show the agent retrying the same blocked call several times before giving up. What should change?
why: Say why the call was blocked and what unblocks it, so the agent calls verify_identity instead of retrying.
Right when an action is waiting on someone. Here the agent needs to take a step first.
Right when handing work to a person. The agent can fix this itself.
The gate already enforces the order. The agent's problem is that it can't tell what the gate wants.

members.stem: Refunds over $500 need a manager's approval. The agent routes them for approval correctly, but sometimes tells customers “your refund is on its way” before anyone has approved it. What should change?
why: Right when a call is blocked by a missing step. This one went through and is waiting.
An explicit pending status makes the agent tell the customer the true state, not a generic success.
Right when handing work to a person. The customer is the one being misinformed here.
Right for soft preferences. What the customer is told about money needs to be accurate every time.

members.stem: When the CI agent can't fix a failing test, it posts “Could not fix this test” on the PR, and engineers start their investigation from scratch. What should it post instead?
why: Right when an agent's call is blocked. Here the agent is handing the work to people.
Right when work is waiting on approval. Here engineers need to take over.
Give the humans the failure, the hypothesis, what was tried and what to do next, so they don't start over.
Right when steps run in the wrong order. Here the problem is an empty handoff.

options: Keep routing results through the coordinator so it can check coverage.
Pass each subagent only its goal, constraints and the relevant prior findings.
Have independent subagents run in parallel within the same turn.
Give the coordinator a cap on research rounds before it synthesizes.

members.stem: To save a hop, a teammate proposes letting the search subagent send its results straight to the synthesis subagent, bypassing the coordinator. Coverage gaps have been the system's main quality problem. What should the team do?
why: The coordinator can only spot gaps and re-delegate if results pass through it.
Right when subagents get too much context. This is about where results go.
Right when independent work runs one after another. Saving a hop isn't worth losing the coverage check.
Right when the coordinator won't stop. Here the concern is coverage.

members.stem: For “context,” the coordinator passes every subagent the user's full 30-turn conversation. Subagents get distracted by side topics and run slowly. What should the coordinator pass instead?
why: Right when results bypass the coordinator. The problem here is what goes into each subagent.
Give each subagent what its task needs, and no more.
Right when independent work runs one after another. Each subagent is slow here because of its input.
Right when the coordinator loops too long. The problem here is the input.

options: Resume the earlier session by its ID with --resume.
Resume, and tell Claude which files changed so it re-reads only those.
Start a fresh session seeded with a short summary of the findings.
Fork the session to try a different approach from the same point.

members.stem: A CI review step runs claude -p --output-format json. A later step must apply the suggested fixes with the full context of that review, and nothing has changed in between. How do you carry the context over?
why: Read session_id from the first step's JSON output and pass it to --resume in the second step.
Right when files changed since the session. Nothing changed here.
Right when the old context is stale or too long. Here it's exactly what the next step needs.
Right for exploring an alternative. Here the next step continues the same work.

members.stem: You resume yesterday's investigation session. Since then a teammate changed 3 of the 40 files Claude analyzed; the rest are untouched. What's the most efficient reliable approach?
why: Resuming alone leaves Claude trusting stale reads of the 3 changed files.
Keep the valid context, and point Claude at the specific files that are now stale.
Right when most of the context is stale. Here 37 of 40 files are unchanged.
Right for trying an alternative approach. Here the work continues, with 3 files updated.
